concepts.topicTitle: Tissues and why plant and animal tissues differ
concepts.label: Tissues and the Hierarchy of Organisation
concepts.cardText: In all multicellular organisms there is a hierarchy of organisation. Cells of similar type performing similar function group together to form a tissue, more than one type of tissue forms organs, different organs form organ systems and organ systems form an organism. In unicellular organisms such as amoeba a single cell performs all the functions of life, but in multicellular organisms different groups of cells perform different functions. A tissue is a group of cells, similar in structure, that work together to perform a specific function. Different types of tissues lead to division of labour, which increases the efficiency of the body and enables it to carry out complex life processes. In animals muscle tissue enables movement and nervous tissue carries messages; in plants xylem transports water and minerals while phloem transports food.

concepts.topicTitle: Tissues and why plant and animal tissues differ
concepts.label: Why Are Plant and Animal Tissues Different?
concepts.cardText: Most plants are fixed in one place and do not move like animals, so they need support to stay firm and upright; plant cells have a cell wall that provides rigidity and strength. In general animals can move, and without a rigid cell wall animal cells can change shape easily, a flexibility that helps make their bodies suitable for locomotion. Modes of nutrition also differ: animals have tissues that help digest food from different sources, while plants have tissues that use solar energy to make food by photosynthesis. Plants and animals have distinct tissues for transporting food and water, and their growth patterns vary because the tissues responsible for growth differ in structure and function.

concepts.label: Meristematic Tissue and Plant Growth
concepts.cardText: A small seedling grows into a tall tree, roots grow deep into the soil, stems become thicker with time and grass grows again after being eaten by grazing animals. Plants grow in three ways: an increase in length (height of stem and depth of roots), an increase in girth (thickness of stem), and regrowth after cutting the branches or grazing by animals. This growth requires actively dividing cells that together form a tissue called a meristematic tissue.

concepts.label: Apical Meristem: Growth in Length
concepts.cardText: In Activity 3.1 two onion bulbs are placed in jars of water and their roots measured; on day 3 the root tips of the bulb in Jar B are cut by about 1 cm. Roots in Jar A continue to grow in length while roots in Jar B stop growing after the tips are cut. This shows that roots grow only from their tips, which consist of cells that divide continuously, as seen earlier as mitosis in onion root tips. Shoot tips also contain actively dividing cells that help the shoots to grow in length. So plants have growth zones at the tips of their roots and shoots, called the apical meristems, which help the plants grow in length.

concepts.label: Lateral Meristem and Annual Rings: Growth in Girth
concepts.cardText: The stems of dicot plants not only grow in length but also increase in diameter or girth over time. On the cut trunk of a tree there are ring-like patterns called annual growth rings. Some rings are wide and some narrow, reflecting favourable or unfavourable growth conditions during a particular year, and by counting them scientists can estimate the age of a tree and understand the climatic conditions under which it grew. The increase in girth occurs due to actively dividing cells arranged in a ring in the stem. These cells divide and produce new cells inside and outside in a concentric manner, leading to an increase in diameter of the stem. This meristematic tissue is called the lateral meristem.

concepts.label: Intercalary Meristem: Regrowth After Cutting
concepts.cardText: If the tip of a young stem is cut, the stem stops growing in length but new branches arise from the nodes. The node is the point on a plant stem where branches or leaves arise, and the part of the stem between two nodes is the internode. The intercalary meristem is located at the base of the internode or just above the node. When a garden hedge is cut more branches appear again, and grass reappears after being mowed or grazed, because of the intercalary meristem at the nodes of its stem. So plants have three types of meristematic tissue: the apical meristem at the root and shoot tips increases length, the lateral meristem along the circumference of stems increases girth, and the intercalary meristem at the base of certain plants such as grasses helps them regenerate after cutting. Together these account for growth in length, girth and branching.

concepts.label: Meristematic Cells and Differentiation
concepts.cardText: The cells of meristematic tissues are small, have thin cell walls, a large and prominent nucleus, and dense cytoplasm with many organelles. Vacuoles are generally absent and the cells are tightly packed with little or no intercellular space. These characteristics allow continuous and rapid cell division. Due to continuous division, meristematic tissue adds new cells to the plant body. Some of the newly formed cells remain meristematic while others lose the ability to divide. The cells that lose the ability to divide change in structure and function and become permanent tissues, specialised to perform functions such as support, transport or storage. This process, by which meristematic tissue becomes specialised to perform specific functions, is called differentiation.

concepts.label: Permanent Tissues: Simple and Complex
concepts.cardText: A transverse section of a sunflower stem shows different groups of cells, and each tissue is specialised to perform a specific function. These are permanent tissues. Permanent tissues can be simple, composed of only one type of cell, or complex, composed of more than one type of cell. Functionally, the chapter studies protective tissue (epidermis), supporting tissue (the simple permanent tissues parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma) and conducting tissues (the complex permanent tissues xylem and phloem).

concepts.label: Epidermis: Protective Tissue
concepts.cardText: The epidermis forms the outermost layer of the plant body. It consists of a tightly packed, single layer of flat and rectangular cells and protects all parts of the plant. These cells are covered with a waxy layer of cutin called the cuticle. In plants of very dry habitats the cuticle may be thick to reduce water loss through transpiration. In roots, hair-like projections called root hair increase the surface area for absorption of water and minerals from the soil. In leaves the epidermis has pores called stomata, which apart from gaseous exchange help in transpiration, the evaporation of water vapour. Transpiration helps water transportation by creating a transpiration pull in xylem, and also helps eliminate wastes from the plant body.

concepts.label: Parenchyma: Storage and Floating
concepts.cardText: Supporting tissues, which are simple permanent tissues, are of three types: parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma. Parenchyma consists of living cells with thin walls that are loosely packed with intercellular spaces. It mainly stores food but also performs photosynthesis in the green parts of plants. In aquatic plants specialised parenchyma forms air spaces, which help them float.

concepts.label: Xylem: Conducting Water and Minerals
concepts.cardText: Plants have specialised conducting tissues called xylem and phloem, together known as complex permanent tissues because they are made up of different types of cells working together. Xylem is the tissue that transports water and minerals from the roots to other parts of the plant, and it also provides strength. Xylem consists of tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres. Tracheids and vessels are tubular and thick-walled. Xylem parenchyma are the only living component of xylem, while tracheids, vessels and xylem fibres are primarily sclerenchymatous.

concepts.label: Phloem: Conducting Food
concepts.cardText: Unlike the xylem, phloem is mostly made up of living cells. It consists of sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres. Some cells are long and tubular, joined end to end by perforated walls, and these form sieve tubes, which transport food from leaves to other parts of the plant. The cellular functions of the sieve tube cells are regulated by companion cells, which are specialised parenchyma cells whose main function is to monitor loading and unloading of sugars in sieve tubes. Phloem parenchyma store food materials, and resin, tannins and latex. The sieve tubes are also supported by phloem fibres, which provide strength.

concepts.label: Tissue Systems in Plants
concepts.cardText: In a plant body the tissues do not work alone; they are organised together into larger groups called tissue systems. Plant tissues are organised into three tissue systems. The dermal tissue system forms the outer covering of the plant, protects the inner parts and reduces water loss. The ground tissue system forms the main body of a plant between the dermal and conducting tissues and includes parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma. The vascular tissue system consists of the conducting tissues, xylem and phloem. Plant tissues are also broadly classified into meristematic and permanent tissues, depending on their ability to divide.

concepts.label: Epithelial Tissue
concepts.cardText: Epithelial tissue forms the outer covering of the body (skin) and also lines the internal organs, such as the mouth, lungs, blood vessels and intestine. It is composed of closely packed cells with very little space between them. This structure prevents the entry of germs, reduces water loss, and also helps in the absorption, secretion and movement of substances. Different types of epithelial tissue are structurally adapted to perform different functions. In the lungs the epithelium is suited to gas exchange, and epithelial tissue lining internal organs is usually only one or a few cells thick to allow quick exchange of materials.

concepts.label: Connective Tissue: Blood and Bone
concepts.cardText: A tissue that connects and supports other tissues is called a connective tissue. Blood and bones are both connective tissues, but they differ in composition and consistency: blood is fluid while bone is hard, a difference due to the matrix, which is soft and jelly-like in blood but hard, solid and rigid in bones. The red colour of blood is due to haemoglobin, an iron-rich protein in the Red Blood Cells (RBCs), which live for about 4 months and are replaced regularly. Platelets help in blood clotting at the site of an injury. During exercise muscles need more oxygen, so breathing becomes faster and blood flow increases. White Blood Cells (WBCs) collect at infected areas, causing pus formation and inflammation.

concepts.label: Muscle Tissue: Skeletal, Smooth and Cardiac
concepts.cardText: Movements under our conscious control, such as running, writing or lifting objects, are voluntary movements carried out by skeletal muscles, which are attached to the skeleton. They are made of bundles of long cylindrical muscle fibres that are unbranched, multinucleate and striated. Many movements occur automatically without conscious control, such as the movement of food in the intestine and the beating of the heart; these are involuntary movements. Smooth muscles are found in organs like the stomach and intestines; their cells are spindle-shaped, have a single nucleus and lack striations, and they help in slow, continuous movements like digestion. Cardiac muscles are found only in the heart; their fibres are cylindrical and branched with a single nucleus and have faint striations, and they work tirelessly and rhythmically so the heart beats throughout life without fatigue.

concepts.label: Nervous Tissue and Neurons
concepts.cardText: Actions such as pulling your hand away from something hot are controlled by nervous tissue, which forms the body's control and coordination network. The brain acts as the control centre, coordinating activities, memory and responses across the body. Muscles, both voluntary and involuntary, cannot function independently; they receive instructions from the nervous tissue, for example the brain signals the heart to beat faster during exercise to meet the body's increased oxygen demand. The cells of nervous tissue are neurons, or nerve cells, specialised to receive, process and transmit messages. Each neuron has a cell body that contains the nucleus and controls cell activities, dendrites that receive signals from other neurons, and an axon, a long fibre that carries messages from the cell and ends at axon terminals, which transmit the messages to other cells.

concepts.label: The Musculoskeletal System
concepts.cardText: The musculoskeletal system is made up of bones, muscles, joints, cartilage, tendons and ligaments. It helps us stand upright, move, maintain posture and protect delicate organs, and it functions under the control of the nervous system. Muscles pull on bones to produce movement. They are attached to bones by strong, flexible bands called tendons. When a muscle contracts, the tendon transmits this force to the bone, resulting in movement at a joint. On average the adult human skeleton makes up about 12 to 15 per cent of body weight. A joint is a junction between two or more bones; joints allow movement but cannot move the bones on their own.

concepts.label: Types of Joints
concepts.cardText: Some parts of the body move easily in many directions while others move only in one direction, and the difference is due to the types of joints present. The shoulder is a ball and socket joint: the rounded top of the upper arm bone fits into a shallow hollow of the shoulder bone, allowing forward, backwards, sideways and circular movements. The elbow is a hinge joint, bending and straightening in one direction only like a door hinge; the knee is also a hinge joint, where the kneecap protects the joint. The skull is connected to the backbone through a pivot joint, which allows the head to move side to side like a doorknob turning in its socket. The bones of the skull are connected by fixed joints, which cannot move, keeping the brain safe even when the body moves.

concepts.label: The Skeletal System
concepts.cardText: The skeletal system consists of a framework of bones that provides strength and protects delicate internal organs. It includes the skull, vertebral column and rib cage. The backbone or vertebral column (spine) is made up of a series of small bones called vertebrae, supports the body and helps us stand upright. Between each vertebra is a cartilage disc that acts as a cushion and allows flexibility, so we can bend and twist without injuring the internal spinal cord. There are 12 pairs of ribs, which together form the rib cage that protects vital organs such as the heart and lungs. The ribs are attached to the spine at the back and to the breast bone (sternum) in front and are joined by flexible cartilage, which allows the rib cage to expand and contract during breathing so that air moves in and out of the lungs.

concepts.label: Totipotency: From One Cell to an Organism
concepts.cardText: In 1958 F. C. Steward demonstrated that even single cells from the vascular phloem of carrot retain the ability to regenerate whole plants. He grew these cells in a nutrient medium containing simple sugars and hormones under appropriate conditions, and the phloem cells divided to form a mass of cells, which gradually divided and differentiated into a complete plant. This shows that phloem cells first dedifferentiated, regaining the ability to divide, to form an undifferentiated mass of unspecialised cells, which with nutrients and growth chemicals further divided and redifferentiated to form roots, shoot and eventually the complete plant. Thus some mature plant cells can undifferentiate, divide and redifferentiate to develop into a new plant under specific conditions. This is known as totipotency and such cells are totipotent cells, similar to the ability of a zygote to divide and differentiate into an entire organism.

concepts.label: Crown Gall Disease and Agrobacterium
concepts.cardText: In crown gall disease, tumour-like swellings develop on plant stems due to rapid and uncontrolled cell division, caused by a bacterium called Agrobacterium tumefaciens. Instead of only trying to cure the disease, scientists studied how the bacterium transfers its genetic material into plant cells. This knowledge was later used in plant tissue culture and genetic engineering. Today Agrobacterium is used as a tool to introduce useful genes into plants for the production of valuable phytochemicals, improved crops and disease-resistant varieties.
